meta.title: Mia's Fact File: Seahorses
meta.textType: functional: an animal fact file, a blog post

paragraphs: Posted by Mia. On Saturday, the Explorers went to the town aquarium, and I saw a seahorse for the first time. A keeper held a ruler next to the glass, and I took a photo. The seahorse moved only once in ten minutes. I love animals, so I wanted to learn more about this one. Here are the facts for my fact file. Teacher Kim will read my post first, and then she will put it on the blog.

Where seahorses live. Wild seahorses live in the warm, shallow sea. The ocean is enormous, but seahorses stay near the coast. They hold sea grass with their curled tails. In this way, the water does not take them away. A seahorse spends its whole life in the sea. The grass hides the seahorses from big fish. It does not swim fast, and it does not move much. Some people think that a seahorse is an insect or a horse, but it is a fish.

What seahorses eat. A seahorse eats a lot of tiny animals every day. It has no teeth, so it eats its food whole. How big is a seahorse? The seahorse at the aquarium is about twelve centimeters tall. It weighs about nine grams, and that is much less than one mango.

Why seahorses are special. There are about forty kinds of seahorses, and they have various colors. Some are yellow, some are orange, and some are brown. The seahorse at the aquarium is yellow. I think that it is beautiful. The father carries the eggs in a pouch, a small bag on his body. He carries them for about two weeks. When the babies are ready, they leave the pouch and swim away. Birds make a nest in a tree, but a seahorse does not make a nest. Did you know that?

Lily read this post over my shoulder. "A few facts are new to me," she said. I have a little time before dinner, so I will draw the father with his pouch. Which animal do you like best? Please tell us in the comments. P.S. Nadia asked me about seahorses, so this post is for her.
text.summary: Mia writes a blog post about the seahorse that she saw at the aquarium. It has three headings and tells where seahorses live, what they eat, and why the father seahorse is special.
